pr.title: Revert: create const block bodies in typeck via query feeding
pr.description:
as per the discussion in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/125806#discussion_r1622563948

It was a mistake to try to shoehorn const blocks and some specific anon consts into the same box and feed them during typeck. It turned out not simplifying anything (my hope was that we could feed `type_of` to start avoiding the huge HIR matcher, but that didn't work out), but instead making a few things more fragile.

reverts the const-block-specific parts of https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/124650

@bors rollup=never had a small perf impact previously

fixes https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/125846

r? @compiler-errors
pr.author: oli-obk

processing.reason: The PR’s historically incorrect transformation is a compiler-representation/ICE regression: inline const blocks lacked their own AST-lowered HIR body/DefId, so the added regression test is `//@ check-pass` and only verifies that compilation no longer ICEs. The patch changes body ownership, typeck/writeback, MIR-key collection, and liveness traversal, but contains no source-level value assignment or runtime-semantics change (the host-decoded MIR diff has no changed hunks). Constructing two Miri-valid Rust functions that return different values would therefore require inventing an unrelated value-level rewrite, which the task forbids. The correct historical difference is compile success versus ICE, not differing defined executions.

analysis.summary: Historical inline-const body handling was reverted after lazily creating const-block DefIds/bodies during typeck, guarded by a `has_inline_consts` cache, made HIR/MIR/liveness handling fragile and caused an ICE for inline const patterns. The corrected model gives every const block a real HIR body and DefId during AST lowering, includes those bodies in normal body-owner iteration, and typechecks each body in its own function context.
analysis.originalLogic: Inline const blocks were represented during HIR lowering as an inner expression, with their `DefId` and body effectively deferred until typeck/writeback. `mir_keys` collected inline-const bodies by loading `tcx.typeck(def_id).inline_consts` only when a cached `has_inline_consts` flag said the body contained them. Typeck handled a const block by checking the inner expression directly: `ExprKind::ConstBlock(ref block) => self.check_expr_with_expectation(block, expected)`. Writeback then created a new `DefKind::InlineConst` def via `tcx.create_def`, mapped its HIR id, and inserted it into `typeck_results.inline_consts`.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: The historically incorrect transformation was the const-block-specific optimization/rework that tried to “shoehorn const blocks and some specific anon consts into the same box and feed them during typeck”: const blocks no longer received their own AST-lowering body/DefId, MIR key collection was gated on a `has_inline_consts` cache, and typeck/writeback synthesized const-block defs and queried the inner expression instead of typechecking a distinct const-block body. The PR explicitly says this “was a mistake” and “instead making a few things more fragile.”
analysis.inputDomain: Rust source containing inline const blocks, especially inline const patterns (`const { ... }` in pattern position under `#![feature(inline_const_pat)]`) whose bodies contain local bindings/statements and borrow/deref expressions, e.g. `let a = 10_usize; *&a`. More generally, any inline const expression whose body must be visited by HIR body-owner collection, liveness/dead-code analysis, MIR construction, or const-context checks.
analysis.trigger: An inline const block is used in pattern position, and its body contains a local binding plus a borrow/deref expression. With the historical deferred-body representation, liveness/MIR-related logic encountered a const block without its own HIR body, which “used to ICE because const blocks didn't have a body anymore.”
preconditions: The program uses inline const blocks (`const { ... }`), at minimum an inline const pattern under `#![feature(inline_const_pat)]`.
The inline const body contains nontrivial body logic such as `let` bindings and `*&a`, rather than only a literal.
The compiler representation has const blocks without their own AST-lowered body/DefId and relies on typeck-created `inline_consts` plus the `has_inline_consts` cache.
Passes that walk body owners, patterns, liveness, or MIR keys assume every const block has a normal HIR body.
pitfalls: Do not treat const blocks as merely an inner expression: they need real `hir::ConstBlock { hir_id, def_id, body }` storage so all HIR visitors can recurse through `visit_inline_const`.
Do not gate MIR body collection of inline consts on a cached `has_inline_consts` flag; collect const-block bodies as regular body owners instead.

Typechecking a const block must use its own body and a fresh `FnCtxt`, then write the resulting type back to the const block's HIR id; simply calling `check_expr_with_expectation` on the inner expression is insufficient.
Writeback must visit the const block's nested body and node id, not manufacture a new `DefKind::InlineConst` definition and record it in a side map.

Passes such as liveness, loops, dead-code, and const checking must have explicit nested-body handling for inline consts; otherwise pattern-position const blocks can ICE or produce wrong usage/liveness results.
The revert also restored nested-body behavior for region resolution, upvar analysis, and `is_inside_const_context`; these are part of the same body-ownership invariant, not unrelated cleanup.
analysis.testStrategy: Add a UI `//@ check-pass` regression test using `#![feature(inline_const_pat)]` with an inline const pattern whose body has local statements and a borrow/deref, matching the historical test shape: `match 0 { const { let a = 10_usize; *&a } | _ => {} }`. This specifically exercises the missing-const-block-body ICE. Also check that unpretty/pretty and MIR-name expectations are updated when const blocks get real bodies, and avoid asserting execution—compile/check-pass is sufficient for the ICE regression.
evidence: It was a mistake to try to shoehorn const blocks and some specific anon consts into the same box and feed them during typeck.
It turned out not simplifying anything
but instead making a few things more fragile.
